name: Royal Victoria Patriotic Building
text: Your train passes near the Royal Victoria Patriotic Building, on the train's {side}, built in 1859 beside Wandsworth Common as a school for girls orphaned in the Crimean War. In the Second World War it became the London Reception Centre, where 34,000 people arriving from occupied Europe were questioned to find spies among them.

name: Battersea Railway Bridge
text: Your train crosses the Thames on Battersea Railway Bridge, dating from 1863 and one of the oldest crossings of the river in London. It was first called the Cremorne Bridge, after the Cremorne pleasure gardens in Chelsea, and once carried broad-gauge track for Great Western trains to Victoria.

name: Stamford Bridge
text: Your train passes near Stamford Bridge, on the train's {side}, home of Chelsea since the club was founded in 1905. The ground opened in 1877 for the London Athletic Club, and its record crowd, 82,905, came to see Chelsea play Arsenal in 1935.

name: Earls Court Exhibition Centre
text: Your train passes the site of the Earls Court Exhibition Centre, on the train's {side}, an art moderne hall built between 1935 and 1937. For decades it hosted the Royal Tournament, the Ideal Home Show and Crufts, and events of the 1948 Olympics; its demolition was finished in 2017.

name: Olympia
text: Your train passes near Olympia, on the train's {side}, which opened in 1886, built as the National Agricultural Hall. Its Grand Hall, with an iron roof made by Handyside of Derby, is listed at Grade II*.

name: White City Stadium
text: Your train passes near the site of White City Stadium, on the train's {side}, built in 10 months for the 1908 Olympics and demolished in 1985. The Olympic marathon finished there, and the race's distance was fixed at those Games, measured from a start at Windsor Castle.

name: Stonebridge Park power station
text: Your train passes near the site of Stonebridge Park power station, on the train's {side}, built in 1913 to 1914 by the London and North Western Railway. From 1914 until 1967 it made the electricity for the suburban electric trains between Euston and Watford.

name: Hirst Research Centre
text: Your train passes near the Hirst Research Centre, on the train's {side}, set up by the General Electric Company and formally opened in 1923 as one of the first specialised industrial research laboratories built in Britain. In the Second World War its engineers made the cavity magnetron far more powerful, helping to make radar small enough to fit in fighter aircraft.

name: The Windermere, South Kenton
text: Your train passes near the Windermere, on the train's {side}, a pub built in about 1938 and listed at Grade II. Its interior is on the Campaign for Real Ale's National Inventory of Historic Pub Interiors.

name: Northwick Park
text: Your train passes near Northwick Park, on the train's {side}, for centuries part of Sheepcote Farm in the manor of Harrow. The land passed to Harrow School, and in the 1930s Middlesex County Council bought 192 acres of it from the school for a public park.

name: Harrow Skate Park
text: Your train passes near Harrow Skate Park, on the train's {side}, opened on July 15th 1978. It is one of only two concrete skateparks from the 1970s still in use in Britain, and its pool was modelled on one in Spring Valley, California.

name: Kodak Harrow works
text: Your train passes near Kodak's former Harrow works, on the train's {side}, opened in 1891 as the company's first factory outside the United States. At its peak in the mid-20th century it employed up to 6,000 people; film-making ended in 2005 and the plant closed in 2016.

name: Hatch End station
text: Your train passes Hatch End station, rebuilt in 1911 to a design by the architect Gerald Horsley. It opened as Pinner, and took its present name in 1956; Bakerloo line trains called here from 1917 until 1982.

name: Wembley Central Mosque
text: Your train passes near Wembley Central Mosque, on the train's {side}, built in 1904 as St Andrew's Presbyterian Church, in a style influenced by the Arts and Crafts movement. With the Muslim Welfare Association next door, it can hold up to 2,200 people.

name: Ace Cafe
text: Your train passes near the Ace Cafe, on the train's {side}, opened in 1938 for traffic on the new North Circular Road and famous in motorcycle culture. It closed in 1969 and reopened on the same site in 1997.

name: Our Lady of Willesden Church
text: Your train passes near Our Lady of Willesden Church, on the train's {side}, a Catholic church built from 1929 to 1931 in the Romanesque Revival style. It houses a shrine to Our Lady of Willesden, whose statue dates from 1892.

name: Park Ward works
text: Your train passes near the former works of Park Ward, on the train's {side}, a coachbuilder founded in 1919 that made car bodies for Bentley and Rolls-Royce. Rolls-Royce bought it in 1939, and in 1961 it merged with H. J. Mulliner to become Mulliner Park Ward.

name: Eden Studios
text: Your train passes near where Eden Studios stood, on the train's {side}, a recording studio in Beaumont Road, Chiswick, from 1972 until it closed in 2007. Elvis Costello, Madness, the Smiths and Kylie Minogue are among those who recorded there; the site was then cleared for housing.

name: Gunnersbury Triangle
text: Your train passes near Gunnersbury Triangle, on the train's {side}, a patch of woodland hemmed in by three railway lines. In 1983 it became the first place in Britain where a public inquiry stopped building because of the land's value for nature, and it opened as a nature reserve in 1985.

name: The National Archives
text: Your train passes near the National Archives at Kew, on the train's {side}, the UK government's official archive, whose first building here was opened by Queen Elizabeth II in 1977. Its records span 1,000 years, from Domesday Book to the present, and the site was once a First World War hospital.

name: Kensal Green Cemetery
text: Your train passes near Kensal Green Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1833 and one of London's 'Magnificent Seven' cemeteries. Among those buried there are the engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel and the novelists William Makepeace Thackeray and Anthony Trollope.

name: Kensal Rise Library
text: Your train passes near Kensal Rise Library, on the train's {side}, opened by Mark Twain in 1900 on land given by All Souls College, Oxford. When it was threatened with closure, Alan Bennett, Philip Pullman and Zadie Smith were among those who campaigned to save it.

name: Islamia Primary School
text: Your train passes near Islamia Primary School, on the train's {side}, founded in 1983 by the singer Yusuf Islam, known before as Cat Stevens. In 1998 it became the first Muslim school in Britain to be granted public funding, after a campaign of 13 years.

name: Kiln Theatre
text: Your train passes near the Kiln Theatre, on the train's {side}, opened on Kilburn High Road in 1980 as the Tricycle and renamed in 2018. It became known for plays made from the words spoken at public inquiries, as well as new writing.

name: Decca Studios
text: Your train passes near the former Decca Studios, on the train's {side}, at 165 Broadhurst Gardens, where Decca made its recordings from 1937. David Bowie recorded his first single there in 1964, and the Zombies their hit 'She's Not There'.

name: JW3
text: Your train passes near JW3, on the train's {side}, the Jewish Community Centre London, opened on Finchley Road in 2013. Its name plays on its postcode, NW3, and the idea came from Vivien Duffield's visit to a Jewish community centre in Manhattan in 2003.

name: Keats House
text: Your train passes near Keats House, on the train's {side}, where the poet John Keats lodged from 1818 to 1820. According to his friend Charles Brown, 'Ode to a Nightingale' was written under a plum tree in the garden, and here Keats fell in love with Fanny Brawne, who lived next door.

name: Parliament Hill Lido
text: Your train passes near Parliament Hill Lido, on the train's {side}, an open-air pool first opened in 1938. It is unheated and open all year, though from September to April only for early-morning swims.

name: Little Green Street
text: Your train passes Little Green Street, on the train's {side}, a tiny Kentish Town street of houses built in the 1780s, eight on one side and two on the other. It is one of the few intact Georgian streets left in London, and its houses are listed at Grade II.

name: Camden Town Brewery
text: Your train passes over Camden Town Brewery, which began brewing in 2010 in five Victorian railway arches beneath Kentish Town West station. Its founder, Jasper Cuppaidge, first brewed at The Horseshoe, his pub in Hampstead, using one of his grandfather's recipes.

name: Whittington Park
text: Your train passes near Whittington Park, on the train's {side}, named, like the nearby Whittington Hospital, after Dick Whittington. A large topiary cat, after his legendary pet, stands at the Holloway Road entrance.

name: Harringay Arena
text: Your train passes near the site of Harringay Arena, on the train's {side}, an eight-sided arena put up in eight months in 1936. It held the basketball and wrestling of the 1948 Olympics and Billy Graham's first crusade in Britain in 1954, and closed in 1958.

name: Railway Fields
text: Your train passes near Railway Fields, on the train's {side}, a railway goods yard until 1967 and now a nature reserve of about one hectare. More than 200 kinds of wild flower have been recorded there, among them the Haringey knotweed, a hybrid first found in 1987.

name: Konk
text: Your train passes near Konk, on the train's {side}, the recording studio the Kinks set up in Hornsey in the early 1970s, a mile from their home ground of Muswell Hill. Ray and Dave Davies paid for it partly with money from hits such as 'Lola', and the band recorded there full-time from about 1973.

name: St Mary's Tower, Hornsey
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Tower, on the train's {side}, all that is left of Hornsey's medieval parish church and the oldest building in Hornsey. Its date isn't known; the antiquarian Daniel Lysons seems to have been the first to put it at about 1500.

name: Bluebell Wood
text: Your train passes near Bluebell Wood, on the train's {side}, just over an acre of oak wood that is the last fragment of Tottenham Wood, which covered about 388 acres in 1619. Despite its name, no native bluebells grow there.

name: Friern Hospital
text: Your train passes near the former Friern Hospital, on the train's {side}, opened in 1851 as Colney Hatch Lunatic Asylum. At its height it held 2,500 patients and had the longest corridor in Britain; it closed in 1993 and became housing.

name: New Barnet War Memorial
text: Your train passes near New Barnet War Memorial, on the train's {side}, built in 1921 with a bronze figure of winged victory on top. It names 277 men and one woman of the district who died in the First World War; 136 names from the Second World War were added later.

name: Monken Hadley Common
text: Your train passes near Monken Hadley Common, on the train's {side}, a wedge of common land between Monken Hadley and Cockfosters. It is a remnant of the royal forest of Enfield Chase, enclosed by an Act of Parliament in 1777.

name: Bounds Green tube station
text: Your train passes near Bounds Green tube station, on the train's {side}, opened in 1932 on the Piccadilly line's extension to Cockfosters. Its eight-sided entrance was designed by C. H. James in the style of Charles Holden, a well-preserved example of London Transport's modern look of the 1930s.
